title: Charts, Sources and Research
bigQuestion: How do you find out something true that nobody in the room already knows?

story.title: The Yearbook in the Closet
story.kicker: A class wants to know when their school got its name. The answer is not online. It is in a dusty box.
paragraphs: Ms. Reyes's class had a question nobody could answer. "Why is our school called Harper Elementary?" Nate said it was named after a basketball player. Zoe said it was a mayor. The principal shrugged. "It was before my time." So the class decided to find out.

First they tried the internet. One website said the school opened in 1961. Another said 1958. A third had a picture of a totally different Harper school in another state. "Three answers," Ms. Reyes said. "That means we do not have one yet."

Then the librarian remembered a box in the closet. Inside were old yearbooks. The oldest was from 1959. On the first page was a photo of a woman in glasses and a note: "Our school is named for Dr. Alma Harper, who taught in this town for forty years." It was signed by the first principal.

"This is a primary source," Ms. Reyes said. "It was made at the time, by someone who was there." The websites were secondary. They were written later, by people who had never seen this page. Zoe wrote the fact in her notebook, in her own words, and wrote "Harper yearbook, 1959, page 1" beside it.

The class made a chart of every source they had used and how much they trusted each one. The yearbook went at the top. The website with the wrong school went at the bottom. Nate was a little sad it was not a basketball player. But now he knew something true that no one in the building had known.
story.think: Three websites gave three different answers. Why did the class trust the old yearbook more than any of them?

lessons.title: Reading a Chart or Graph
lessons.mainIdea: A chart or graph is a text made of shapes and numbers, so read its title, its labels and its key before you read its bars or lines.
reading: A bar *chart* about Harper Elementary shows five bars. The title says "Students at Harper by Year." The bottom says the years: 1960, 1980, 2000, 2020. The side says "number of students." The tallest bar is 1980. Without reading a sentence, you know the school was biggest in 1980.

Read a chart in this order. Title first: what is this about? Then the *labels* on the bottom and the side: what does each direction mean? Then the *key*, if there is one: what does each color stand for? Only then look at the bars or the line. Readers who skip to the bars often read the chart backward.

A line graph works the same way, but it shows change over time. A line going up means more. A line going down means less. A flat line means no change. Ask the same question you ask of a paragraph: "What is the main idea of this graph?" For the Harper chart, it is "The school grew, then shrank."

words.d: a picture that shows numbers with bars, lines or pieces
a word or number on a chart that tells what a part means
a small box on a chart or map that tells what each color or symbol means

look.title: Students at Harper by Year
look.cite: made-up numbers for a model chart, written for this lesson
look.prompt: What is the main idea of this chart in one sentence? Which year had the most students?

check.q: What should you read first on a chart?
check.why: The title tells what the chart is about. Then labels, then key, then bars.

check.q: On the Harper chart, which year had the most students?
check.why: 1980 has 520 students, the highest number.

check.q: A line on a graph goes down from left to right. What does that mean?
choices: The number is going down over time
check.why: On a line graph, down means less as time passes.

lessons.title: Tables and Maps
lessons.mainIdea: A table lines facts up in rows and columns, and a map shows where; both answer questions if you read their headings and their keys.
reading: A *table* is facts in a grid. The Harper class made one with three columns: Source, What It Said, and How Much We Trust It. Each *row* was one source. To find a fact, run your finger across a row and down a column until they meet. That box is your answer.

A map is a picture of a place from above. The class found a 1960 map of their town. The school was on it, but the big road next to it was not built yet. The key showed a small square for schools and a cross for churches. Read the title, the key and the compass. Then find what you need.

Both tables and maps answer questions fast. "Which source did we trust least?" Look at the trust column. "Was the school near the river in 1960?" Look at the map. A table or a map is a text. It just puts its sentences in boxes and pictures instead of lines.

words.d: facts arranged in rows and columns
one line across a table
the small symbol on a map that shows north, south, east and west

look.title: One Question, One Box
look.text: Picture the class's table. Row one: Harper yearbook, 1959. Row two: Town website. Row three: Website with the wrong school. The trust column says High, Medium, Low. Someone asks, "Which source got Medium?" A student runs her finger down the trust column, stops at Medium, then slides left to the source column.
look.prompt: Which source got a Medium rating? Describe the finger path you would use to find the yearbook's rating.

check.q: How do you find a fact in a table?
choices: Find where the right row and column meet
check.why: A table's answer sits in the box where a row and a column cross.

check.q: What does a map key tell you?
choices: The date the map was made
What each symbol or color means
check.why: The key explains the symbols, like a small square for a school.

check.q: The class map from 1960 did not show the big road. What does that tell you?
check.why: A map shows the place at the time it was made. The road came later.

lessons.title: Primary and Secondary Sources
lessons.mainIdea: A primary source was made at the time by someone who was there; a secondary source was made later by someone who studied it.
reading: The 1959 yearbook was made in 1959, by people who were in the building. It is a *primary source*. A letter, a photo, a diary, a map from that year, a speech, a report card: all primary. They are the closest you can get to being there.

A website written last year about the school's history is a *secondary source*. So is an encyclopedia article or a textbook. The writer was not there. She read primary sources, or other secondary sources, and then wrote her own words. Secondary sources are useful. They gather a lot in one place. But they can pass along mistakes.

Here is the test. Ask, "Was this made at the time, by someone who saw it?" If yes, primary. If it was made later, by someone looking back, secondary. Both kinds have a place. Start with secondary sources to learn the big picture. Then check the facts against a primary source when you can.

words.d: something made at the time of an event by a person who was there
something made later by a person who studied the event
a book or website with short articles on many subjects

look.title: Two Sources, One Day
look.text: Source A: "Dear Mama, the new school opened today. Dr. Harper cut the ribbon herself. It rained but nobody cared." Source B: "Harper Elementary opened in the fall of 1959. The school was named for a local teacher. Its opening day drew a large crowd."
look.cite: written for this lesson: a letter from a student in 1959 and a website written years later
look.prompt: Which source is primary and which is secondary? What does the letter tell you that the website does not?

check.q: Which is a primary source about a school's opening in 1959?
choices: A letter written that day by a student
check.why: The letter was made at the time by someone who was there.

check.q: Why can secondary sources pass along mistakes?
choices: The writer was not there and relies on other sources
check.why: A writer who was not there can copy an error from another source.

check.q: What is a good order for using both kinds?
choices: Check primary sources first, then ignore the rest
Learn the big picture from secondary, then check facts with primary
check.why: Secondary sources give the overview. Primary sources let you check.

lessons.title: Fact or Opinion
lessons.mainIdea: A fact can be checked and shown true or false; an opinion is what someone thinks or feels, and it cannot be proved.
reading: "Harper Elementary opened in 1959." You can check that. You can find the yearbook and see. It is a *fact*. A fact can be true or false, but either way it can be checked. "Harper is the best school in town." Who says? How would you check it? That is an *opinion*.

Opinions often carry words like best, worst, should, beautiful, boring, and I think. Facts often carry numbers, dates and names. But be careful. "The school has the best test scores in the district" sounds like an opinion because of "best." It is really a fact, because scores can be checked.

Opinions are not bad. Writers are allowed to have them. The trouble comes when an opinion dresses up as a fact. "Everyone knows the old gym was better." Everyone? Ask, "Could I check this?" If the answer is no, you are holding an opinion, no matter how sure the writer sounds.

words.d: a statement that can be checked and shown to be true or false
what a person thinks or feels; it cannot be proved true or false

look.title: Sort the Sentences
look.text: Four sentences from a school newsletter: "The new playground opened in April." "It has three slides and a climbing wall." "It is the most fun playground in Illinois." "Every kid should get extra recess to enjoy it." A student says two are facts and two are opinions.
look.prompt: Which two are facts and which two are opinions? What words gave the opinions away?

check.q: What makes a statement a fact?
check.why: A fact can be checked and shown true or false. Sounding sure is not enough.

check.q: "The school has the best test scores in the district." Fact or opinion?
choices: Fact, because scores can be checked
check.why: Even with "best," this can be checked against the real scores, so it is a fact.

check.q: Which sentence is an opinion?
choices: The playground is behind the gym
The playground is the most fun in Illinois
check.why: "Most fun" is a feeling. You cannot check it the way you can count slides.

lessons.title: Asking a Research Question
lessons.mainIdea: A good research question is specific, can be answered with sources, and is something you do not already know.
reading: Ms. Reyes's class started with a question: "Why is our school called Harper?" That is a good *research question*. It is specific. It can be answered by looking at sources. And nobody in the room knew the answer. If they had already known, there would be nothing to research.

Bad research questions come in two sizes. Too big: "What is the history of schools?" You could spend a lifetime on that. Too small: "What color is our school door?" Just go look. A good question sits in the middle. "When did our school get its gym, and why?" You could answer that in a week with a few sources.

Shape your question before you search. Start with a topic: our school. Ask what you wonder: who is it named for? Add a word that makes it specific: why. Then check: can a source answer this? Ms. Reyes says the best questions make you a little nervous, because you truly do not know.

words.d: looking carefully at sources to find out something true
exact and narrow, not vague or too big

look.title: Three Sizes of Question
look.text: Three students write research questions about Lake Michigan. Kim: "What is everything about Lake Michigan?" Dev: "Is Lake Michigan wet?" Sara: "Why did Chicago build a wall of rocks along the lake near our neighborhood?" Ms. Reyes reads all three and circles one.
look.prompt: Which question did she circle? What is wrong with each of the other two?

check.q: What makes "Why is our school called Harper?" a good research question?
choices: It is specific and can be answered with sources
check.why: It is narrow, sources can answer it, and nobody knew the answer yet.

check.q: What is wrong with "What is the history of schools?"
choices: It is too big to answer
It is about the wrong topic
check.why: That question could take a lifetime. A research question needs to be narrower.

check.q: "What color is our school door?" is a weak research question because...
choices: You can just go look; no research needed
check.why: A question you can answer by looking does not need research.

lessons.title: Notes in Your Own Words
lessons.mainIdea: Take research notes as short phrases in your own words, and put quotation marks around anything you copy exactly.
reading: Zoe read the yearbook note: "Our school is named for Dr. Alma Harper, who taught in this town for forty years." She did not copy it. She wrote: "named for Dr. Alma Harper, a teacher here 40 yrs." Short. Her words. That is a research *note*.

Why not copy? Two reasons. First, copying feels like learning but is not. Your hand moves and your brain sleeps. Second, when you write your report, copied notes turn into copied sentences. That is *plagiarism*, using someone's words as if they were yours. Notes in your own words keep you honest without trying.

Sometimes you want the exact words, like the yearbook's line signed by the first principal. Then copy it, put quotation marks around it, and write where it came from. Quotation marks are a promise: these words are not mine. Everything without marks is yours.

words.d: a short phrase you write down to remember a fact
using someone else's words or ideas as if they were your own
the marks around words copied exactly from a source

look.title: The Same Fact, Three Ways
look.text: Source: "The gym was added in 1974 after the old one flooded twice in one spring." Note 1: "The gym was added in 1974 after the old one flooded twice in one spring." Note 2: "gym built 1974, old gym flooded 2x" Note 3: "the old one "flooded twice in one spring" (yearbook 1975, p. 3)"
look.prompt: Which note is a copy with no marks? Which is a good note in the student's own words? Which quotes honestly?

check.q: What is plagiarism?
choices: Using someone's words or ideas as if they were yours
Putting quotation marks around a quote
check.why: Plagiarism is passing off another person's words as your own.

check.q: Which is the best research note for the gym fact?
choices: I think the gym is nice
check.why: It is short, in the student's own words, and keeps the key facts.

check.q: You want to keep the exact words from a source. What must you do?
choices: Change one word so it is yours
Put quotation marks around it and note where it came from
check.why: Quotation marks plus the source is the honest way to keep exact words.

lessons.title: Keeping Track of Sources
lessons.mainIdea: Write down where every fact came from, with the title, the maker, the date and the page or web address, so you and your reader can find it again.
reading: Zoe wrote "Harper yearbook, 1959, page 1" next to her note. Two weeks later, when she wrote her report, she could say exactly where the fact came from. A friend who doubted her could go check. That is why researchers keep track of *sources*.

For each source, write four things. What is it called? Who made it? When was it made? Where did you find it: the page number, or the web address? For the yearbook: "Harper Elementary Yearbook, Harper students, 1959, page 1." For a website: its name, who runs it, the date if you can find it, and the address.

Keep a *source list* on one page. Number each source. Then in your notes, just write the number: "named for Dr. Harper (1)." At the end of your report, print the list. Readers can see you did real work. And if two sources disagree, you know exactly which said what.

words.d: any book, page, picture, person or website where a fact comes from
a numbered list of every source you used, with title, maker, date and place found
the line of letters at the top of a browser that names one page on the internet

look.title: Facts Found in Each Source
look.cite: counted for this lesson, from the class research in the chapter story
look.prompt: Which source gave the class the most facts? Why is it still worth listing the source that gave zero?

check.q: Why write down where a fact came from?
choices: So you or your reader can find and check it later
So you can skip taking notes
check.why: A source note lets anyone go back and check the fact.

check.q: Which four things go in a source entry?
check.why: Title, maker, date and page or address let a reader find the source again.

check.q: Two sources disagree about a date. How does a source list help?
choices: It picks the right date for you
It lets you see exactly which source said what
check.why: With numbered sources, you know which one gave each date and can check both.

lessons.title: A Solid Website or a Shaky One
lessons.mainIdea: Trust a website more when you can tell who made it, when it was made, and where its facts came from; trust it less when it hides those things or makes wild claims.
reading: The class found three websites. One was the town's own site, with the town seal, a date at the bottom, and a phone number. One was a page with no author, no date, and ads flashing everywhere. One had a photo of a different Harper school in another state. Which one would you trust?

Ask three questions. Who made this? A school, a library, a museum, a newspaper or a government office usually has people checking facts. A page with no name has no one to ask. When was it made? A page from ten years ago may be out of date. Where did the facts come from? A solid site tells you. A shaky one just says "trust me."

Watch for warning signs. Spelling mistakes in the title. Claims that sound too big: "the most famous school in America!" Pictures that do not match the words. Also check the site against another source. If the town site and the yearbook agree, you are on solid ground. If a lone site says something no one else says, be careful.

words.d: able to be trusted; a reliable source gets its facts right
old enough that some of the facts may have changed
something a writer says is true

look.title: Three Sites on the Screen
look.text: Site A: "Harper Elementary, official site of the Town of Millbrook. Updated this year. Contact: Town Clerk." Site B: "BEST SCHOOLS EVER!!! Harper opened in 1961 or maybe 1958. No author listed. Click here for free prizes." Site C: a school-history page from a library in another state, with a photo of a Harper High School and a note that it is in Ohio.
look.prompt: Rank the three sites from most to least reliable for the class's question. Give one reason for each rank.

check.q: Which sign makes a website MORE reliable?
choices: It names who made it and when
It says it is the best site ever
check.why: Knowing who made a page and when lets you judge and check it.

check.q: A page has no name and no date and says "trust me." What should you do?
choices: Be careful and check it against other sources
Trust it because it is online
check.why: A source that hides its maker and date needs checking before you use it.

check.q: Why was Site C not useful even though it came from a library?
choices: It was about a different Harper school in another state
check.why: A reliable site can still be about the wrong thing. Always check that it matches your question.

lessons.title: Putting the Answer Together
lessons.mainIdea: Research ends when you can state your answer in your own words, back it with your best sources, and say honestly what you still do not know.
reading: The class wrote its answer: "Harper Elementary is named for Dr. Alma Harper, a teacher who worked in our town for forty years. We know this from the 1959 yearbook, which was written by the first principal. The town website agrees." One sentence of answer. One sentence of source. One sentence of backup.

Notice what the class did not say. It did not say the school opened in 1961. Two websites disagreed, and the yearbook only showed 1959 or earlier. So they wrote, "The school opened in 1959 or a little before. We could not find the exact year." Saying "we could not find" is not failure. It is honesty, and it is what real researchers do.

Go back to the first question and answer it in one breath. Then list your sources. Then name what is still open. That open question, like "What year did it open?", is where the next research starts. Nate is already planning to ask the retired teacher who still lives on Elm Street.

words.d: the facts from sources that back up an answer
truthful; an honest researcher says what is known and what is not

look.title: One Class's Final Answer
look.text: Our school is named for Dr. Alma Harper, who taught here for forty years. Source: the 1959 yearbook, page 1, signed by the first principal. The town website agrees. We do not know the exact year the school opened; two websites give different dates, and no primary source we found gives one.
look.prompt: Which sentence is the answer? Which is the evidence? Which admits what is still unknown?

check.q: What three parts should a research answer have?
choices: A joke, a picture, a title
The answer, the sources, and what is still unknown
check.why: Answer, evidence and the open question make a complete, honest report.

check.q: Why did the class not state the opening year?
choices: The sources disagreed and no primary source gave it
check.why: Two websites gave different years and the yearbook did not settle it, so they said so.

check.q: What is the best thing to do with a question you could not answer?
choices: Leave it out of the report
Say it is unknown and make it the next research question
Pick the website with the nicest photos
check.why: Real researchers say what is open. Open questions are where the next search begins.

review.q: In the class story, why was the 1959 yearbook a primary source?
choices: It was the oldest book in the closet
It was made at the time by people who were there
review.why: A primary source is made at the time by someone who was there.

review.q: What should you read first on a chart?
review.why: The title tells what the chart is about. Then labels, then key, then bars.

review.q: "Harper is the best school in town." What is this?
review.why: "Best" is a feeling that cannot be checked, so it is an opinion.

review.q: Which research question is the right size?
choices: What color is the classroom door?
Why did our town build a new library in 2015?
review.why: It is specific, sources can answer it, and you cannot answer it just by looking.

review.q: You copy a sentence into your notes with no quotation marks and later use it in your report. What is that called?
review.why: Using someone's exact words as your own is plagiarism.

review.q: Which four things go in a source list entry?
choices: First word, last word, page count, font
review.why: Those four let a reader find the source again.

review.q: A website has no author, no date, and says "most famous school in America!" What is it?
choices: Shaky; check it against other sources
review.why: Missing maker and date plus a wild claim are warning signs.

review.q: The class could not find the exact opening year. What did they do?
choices: Said it was unknown and planned more research
Used the website with the wrong school
review.why: Honest research says what is known and what is still open.
